prize_parts.citation: for a visionary body of Romanian prose, with its roots in lyric poetry, in which memory, the body and dream are built into a metaphysical architecture of exceptional formal and imaginative ambition

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged. The citation is narrowed after the exchange. The case rests on the work, not on the fact that all six openings agreed, which is not literary evidence. On public knowledge, the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid make memory, the body and dream into a long, patterned, cumulative imaginative structure, in a voice recognisable within a paragraph. The scale and the decades of sustained effort are what I weigh most. A recurring set of materials is reorganised at different scales and in different forms, which I read as development. In reply to the chair's test question, I would put Solenoid against the earlier Blinding trilogy. The question is whether the later book re-stages the same childhood, body and cosmic material in a new structure and with new intellectual stakes, or only revisits it. That is my reading from public knowledge. I have not verified it against the Romanian text and cannot settle it by assertion. On the scope question, I now favour a citation anchored in the major prose with the poetry named as its lyric origin, not a claim over the whole oeuvre including every early work. Olsson and Palm made that point, and it matches what the translated corpus lets us assess. This lets the citation honour what we can assess, and it stays attributable to a single writer in a single language. The tradition of European modernist epic prose, which he continues and extends, is context for the case, not a substitute for it.
statement.case_against: I will argue the strongest case against, as the chair's last question asks. First, the achievement lies in dense Romanian patterning, wordplay and rhythm. A committee reading mostly through translation could be rewarding a reputation and a recognisable architecture while missing the actual sentences. If the style does not survive translation, we may be honouring something we cannot assess. Second, very long books built on recurring motifs can be insularity, or a closed circuit in which the same images are re-staged at greater length. Third, my own knowledge of the poetry and early work is thinner than my knowledge of the major novels, so any whole-oeuvre wording is less secure than the prose claim. Fourth, I come from the Central European documentary tradition and may find a Central and Eastern European writer congenial. That is a familiarity risk, not evidence of merit. None of these objections is resolved for me. I judge that they weigh less than the voice, scale and sustained imaginative depth, but this is a judgment and could be wrong.

responses.point: Olsson argues that, given Palm's point about uneven coverage of the poetry, the citation should be grounded mainly in the major prose works with the poetry as a related strand. He treats the repetition concern as the real test of this candidacy, one that has to be answered from the books and not from reputation.
responses.response: I now agree with both points and have changed my citation. In round 1 I wrote it to cover prose and poetry equally. I cannot support that evenly from the translated corpus, and the citation should say only what the committee can responsibly assess. It now centres on the prose and names the poetry as its lyric root. On repetition I accept his framing that the test is in the books. My practical suggestion is to compare how Solenoid reorganises the materials of the earlier trilogy. That is a test a reader can actually run, though I have not run it myself.

responses.point: Palm argues that Cărtărescu's effect depends more on large-scale architecture and imagery, which survive translation better, than Michon's depends on French syntax and cadence. She presents this as a judgment about the type of effect, not as verified translation fidelity.
responses.response: I think she is partly right. Architecture and imagery usually travel better than cadence, and that lowers the translation risk relative to Michon. But I would not lean on it too far. Cărtărescu's long patterned syntax is also part of the effect, so some of what we value may be sentence-level and flattened in translation. I therefore treat her argument as reducing the risk, not as removing it. Without a regional or Romanian-language assessment, which the chair's question rightly raises, the translation uncertainty remains open. I would be glad for such an assessment to temper my confidence.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson second but not first because part of the effect lies in book design and in translation and scholarship at the edge of an original oeuvre. She suggests that a citation could be scoped around poetry and lyric-essayistic renewal if defined carefully.
responses.response: That is the formulation I would work from if the committee turned to Carson. A citation naming a renewal of the lyric-essay and a hybrid form of poetry could separate the original work from the translations and the scholarship. The risk I see is that the judgment then depends on how the committee draws the boundary of her oeuvre. For Nox in particular, part of the effect lives in the book as an object, and that is hard to weigh as literary text. I would take her scope seriously as my first alternative, but it needs more drafting work than the Cărtărescu citation. That is why she stays an alternative and is not my first choice.

responses.point: Mattson separates intensity from scale. She sees Michon's voice as strong and recognisable within a sentence, but a small corpus gives less evidence of sustained quality and significance across a body of work. She would want a Michon citation to name precisely what is honoured.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction and with the demand for precision, and it answers the chair's question on Michon. A compact corpus can meet the standard if a citation names what it honours, such as the invention of a form of fictional lives. A small corpus gives the committee less evidence of range, and a style built on syntax loses more in translation. I keep Michon as my second alternative for that reason. If the committee judged that translation obscures too much of Cărtărescu's Romanian, Michon and Carson are where I would look next. Michon's concentrated form would be the better choice if the committee ranked concentrated form above scale. Carson would be the better choice if the committee decided that formal invention across genres can be framed as an oeuvre.

responses.point: Sward holds Can Xue as an alternative because the dream-logic method has an internal rigor, but she wants better evidence of development across the corpus. She asks whether Carson's genre-crossing is the achievement or a vehicle for it.
responses.response: On Can Xue we are close. I ranked her last for the same coverage reason she names, and I cannot say whether the method varies enough across a large output. That is a gap in what I can see, not a verdict on the books. Her Carson question is the useful one, and my answer is that I do not know yet. If the achievement is the form itself, a citation can say so. If it is a vehicle, the scope has to rest on the lyric writing. I would put the same question to Cărtărescu, and there I find the answer clearer, because the innovation lies in the prose itself.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's dense Romanian patterning, wordplay and rhythm survives in the translations available to the committee. No one has claimed command of the originals, and I have not verified any text independently.

Whether the recurrence of motifs across the long novels is deepening or insularity. I read it as development, but only from public knowledge, and the Solenoid test I propose has not been run by me against the text.
Whether the poetry and early work are adequately represented in translation to support even the lyric-roots claim in the citation.

How the committee should weigh Michon's compact corpus and Carson's hybrid, object-based and translated work against an oeuvre standard. I have named conditions under which I would turn to them but have not resolved the question.
My knowledge of Can Xue's untranslated output and of Zurita's non-textual work is limited, so my views on both remain provisional.
Carlberg's simulated vote rests on a modeling assumption about her co-opted status. I draw no conclusion from the count.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level connection is apparent from the supplied profile. My disclosure is unchanged and I restate it. My profile records long engagement with Central Europe, including Prague and Vienna and documentary fiction on Nazism and 20th-century trauma. Cărtărescu writes from Eastern Europe, so this is thematic proximity and not a personal or professional tie. I recognise it as a possible familiarity effect, and in this round I have set out the strongest case against him partly as a check on it. My own literary practice is context, not evidence of preference.
